\title{BoundaryVote: Model-Free Post-Processing for Agricultural Field Boundary Delineation}
\author{Aviskar~Giri and Isaac~Corley%
\thanks{The authors are with Taylor Geospatial, St.\ Louis, MO 63108 USA
(e-mail: aviskar.giri@taylorgeospatial.org).}}
\markboth{IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters}%
{Giri and Corley: BoundaryVote for Agricultural Field Boundary Delineation}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Field boundary networks predict background, field interior, and boundary classes, but those pixels must become polygons to describe individual fields.
On Fields of The World, discarding boundary-class pixels removes thin and small fields, while a watershed, which grows regions from seed points, cuts fields at narrow points without predicted boundaries.
Merging those regions back recovers the accuracy but throws away the correct splits with the wrong ones.
We introduce \emph{BoundaryVote}, which keeps every non-background pixel, over-segments it with a watershed of the boundary probability, and accepts a proposed split only when enough pixels along its line score boundary at least as high as field.
The test compares two of the network's own probabilities at one pixel, so BoundaryVote needs three constants, no weight changes, and no reference polygons at inference.
Across ten held-out countries, polygon-level panoptic quality (PQ), which combines field detection and shape accuracy, rises by \GainMin{} to \GainMax{} points over the post-processing released with Fields of the Planet (FTP), with the same minimum-size step.
The comparison covers two encoders and two sensors, PlanetScope and Sentinel-2, with improvements in \UpTotal{} of 40 country and model pairs at \OursSlowdown{} the FTP pipeline's runtime on the densest patches.
Fields under 0.5~ha, the ones a field-class foreground most often loses and the ones smallholder mapping depends on, gain the most in relative terms.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Agricultural field delineation, instance segmentation, watershed transform, post-processing, remote sensing.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{F}{ield} polygons are the reporting unit for crop area, yield, and management practices, so a field boundary model is only useful once its pixel predictions become one polygon per field.
Public benchmarks now cover this task at 10~m with Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw,dandrimont2023ai4boundaries,persello2023ai4smallfarms} and at 3~m with PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp}.
Models trained on them predict three classes, background, field interior, and boundary~\cite{waldner2020decode,waldner2020edge,kerner2024ftw,muhawenayo2026prue}, most recently for a global map at 10~m~\cite{ftw_global}.
The FTP pipeline~\cite{corley_ftp} uses only field-class pixels as its foreground, the pixels available to form polygons.
Its watershed~\cite{soille2004morphological} starts at peaks in the distance to the nearest predicted boundary pixel~\cite{waldner2020decode,corley_ftp} and uses that distance to divide the foreground.
Before extracting polygons, it merges adjacent regions into connected components.

\label{fig:gallery}

Both pipelines discard boundary-class pixels, so a narrow field or one with uncertain edges disappears when the boundary class covers it (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}).
On PlanetScope with the B3 model, \BaseMiss\% of reference fields have no prediction covering half of their area, and the FTP pipeline predicts fewer fields than the reference in all ten countries.
The watershed introduces another error by placing lines at narrow points in the foreground without checking for a predicted boundary.
Its regions score \RawInstPQ{} PQ against \CCPQ{} for connected components of the same foreground.
Merging the regions back recovers that accuracy, but the FTP pipeline then loses every correct split as well.

We keep boundary-class pixels so that thin and small fields can form polygons, over-segment the foreground with a watershed of the boundary probability seeded at its regional minima, then use the same probabilities to decide which watershed lines to keep.
Each pixel on a line votes for boundary when its boundary probability is at least equal to its field probability, a line's \emph{support} is the share of those votes, and we keep the line only when support reaches $\tau$.
Otherwise, we reject the split and merge the two regions.
We remove the smallest polygons at the end, a minimum-size step any pipeline can apply, and all three constants stay the same for every country and sensor.

We evaluate on the ten densely annotated held-out countries of Fields of The World~\cite{kerner2024ftw} with the EfficientNet~\cite{tan2019efficientnet} U-Nets~\cite{ronneberger2015unet} released with Fields of the Planet~\cite{corley_ftp} for PlanetScope and Sentinel-2, scored against the reference polygons.
With the same minimum-size step, BoundaryVote gains \GainMin{} to \GainMax{} PQ points averaged over countries across two encoders and two sensors, improving \UpTotal{} of the 40 country and model pairs.
Selecting the best watershed depth per country on the test labels recovers at most \OracleGainMax{} of those points (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).

\section{Related Work}
Field delineation from satellite imagery has moved from edge detection and region growing~\cite{wagner2020growing} to fully convolutional networks that predict boundary and interior classes~\cite{persello2019delineation,waldner2020decode,waldner2020edge}.
\emph{A Practical Recipe for Field Boundary Segmentation at Scale} (PRUE)~\cite{muhawenayo2026prue} compared 18 segmentation and geospatial foundation models on Fields of The World, where a U-Net with an EfficientNet encoder outperformed the instance and foundation-model alternatives, and its training recipe produced the PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 models we use.
Fields of the Planet~\cite{corley_ftp} reports that these three-class networks outperform the Delineate Anything instance models~\cite{lavreniuk2025delineateanything}, in both their first and second versions, on the same held-out countries, where the instance models stay below 10 PQ on PlanetScope.
The released field models still assign pixels to three classes before a watershed or connected components produce polygons, so better post-processing helps them without retraining.

Hierarchical merging combines regions in order of border strength until a threshold is reached~\cite{arbelaez2011hierarchical}, as Persello et al.~\cite{persello2019delineation} do for field boundaries.
Stochastic watershed estimates boundary probability by repeating the watershed with randomly sampled seeds~\cite{angulo2007stochastic}, while iterative marker depth methods adjust seed selection for each region~\cite{koyuncu2016iterative}.
Zhu et al.~\cite{zhu2024gfafd} run an oriented watershed on the boundary probability and cut the resulting merge hierarchy at one global level, which they find stable across regions and detection models; we segment the same surface and replace the level with a vote along each line.
Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025earlyseason} fit a two-component Gaussian mixture to a region's extent and boundary probabilities and threshold each at the weighted mean of its component means, without labels.
By checking each line against the network's two class probabilities at the same pixels, we decide splits without a threshold on boundary strength while retaining boundary-class pixels in the foreground.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
To recover the fields this post-processing loses, we start from the network's class probabilities $p_{\mathrm{bg}}, p_{\mathrm{field}}, p_{\mathrm{bnd}}$ for one image (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
BoundaryVote uses only the most probable class at each pixel, written $\arg\max p$, and the field and boundary probabilities to produce field polygons.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{rev_method.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{BoundaryVote keeps boundary-class pixels and rejects splits without predicted boundaries.}
The pixels the network assigns to the boundary class, orange in (c), are the ones the FTP pipeline drops from the foreground and BoundaryVote keeps.
A watershed of the boundary probability, seeded at its regional minima (white in (b)), proposes far too many splits (d).
Colors show support for each proposed line (e), with blue lines following predicted boundaries and red lines crossing fields.
The vote keeps the blue lines and removes the red ones, and the minimum-size step drops the slivers between neighboring kept lines, leaving one polygon per field (f) with the reference outlined in black.
Rows are dense crops, two from PlanetScope and one from Sentinel-2.}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Foreground}
We use $F=\{\arg\max p \neq \mathrm{bg}\}$ as the foreground, keeping both field and boundary classes.
Boundary pixels can then connect neighboring fields, so the watershed must separate them before we extract polygons.

\paragraph{Split Proposals}
We place seeds at the regional minima of $p_{\mathrm{bnd}}$ inside $F$ that are at least $h=0.01$ deep and run a watershed of $p_{\mathrm{bnd}}$ within $F$~\cite{soille2004morphological}, retaining the one-pixel lines between regions.
With seeds in nearly every minimum, the watershed over-segments the foreground: its lines follow every ridge of boundary probability, and they also cross fields wherever the probability dips inside one, leaving the vote to reject those splits.
The FTP pipeline instead segments the distance to the predicted boundary at a seed depth of $h=2$ pixels; we compare both surfaces in Sec.~\ref{sec:ablation}.

\paragraph{The Vote}
For each line $\ell$ separating two regions, every pixel votes for boundary when $p_{\mathrm{bnd}}$ is at least $p_{\mathrm{field}}$ there, and the line's support is the share of those votes,
\begin{equation}
s(\ell)=\frac{1}{|\ell|}\sum_{x\in\ell}\mathbf{1}\left[p_{\mathrm{bnd}}(x)\geq p_{\mathrm{field}}(x)\right],
\label{eq:support}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ equals one when the comparison holds and zero otherwise.
We keep a line with $s(\ell)\geq\tau$ as a one-pixel gap between fields, but remove one with $s(\ell)<\tau$ and merge the two regions.
Regions joined by rejected lines form groups, and we apply all line decisions together.
A line pixel can be filled only when every region it touches joins the same group and no neighboring line pixel would join a different group.
We use $\tau=0.3$, and values from 0.1 to 0.5 change the result by less than half a point (Sec.~\ref{sec:ablation}).

\paragraph{Polygons}
We trace each field's pixel boundary as a polygon without simplifying it.
The one-pixel gaps keep neighbors distinct when the polygons are converted back to pixels on the same grid.
We then drop fields smaller than 900~m$^2$.
Between two kept lines that follow the same thick boundary, the over-segmentation leaves slivers of boundary-class pixels, and this step removes them; without it BoundaryVote scores \OursNoFilterPQ{} PQ (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
The threshold gives the FTP pipeline its highest validation score; BoundaryVote's changes by 0.2 points between 900 and 1800~m$^2$ but drops 1.3 at 450~m$^2$, where slivers survive (supplementary material).

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Data}
We use the test split of the ten densely annotated held-out countries of Fields of The World~\cite{kerner2024ftw}, named in Fig.~\ref{fig:percountry}, with 2,544 PlanetScope patches at 3~m~\cite{corley_ftp} and 3,034 Sentinel-2 patches.
PlanetScope covers only the subset with an aligned PlanetScope image, so we compare each sensor against its own baseline.
We score against the released reference polygons clipped to each patch, rather than class labels on a pixel grid.

\paragraph{Models}
We run the EfficientNet-B3 and B7 U-Nets that Fields of the Planet~\cite{corley_ftp} trained with the PRUE recipe~\cite{muhawenayo2026prue} for PlanetScope and for Sentinel-2.
We use the released weights and average predictions over eight flips and rotations, following the released inference settings.
The Sentinel-2 models run inference on a grid at twice the image resolution, and we score their polygons on that grid.

\paragraph{Baselines}
We reproduce the FTP pipeline using the field class, watershed depth $h=2$, and connected components of the combined regions.
Our per-country PQ agrees with the scores reported by Fields of the Planet~\cite{corley_ftp} to within $10^{-3}$ for both sensors.
To measure what depth tuning can achieve, we also select each country's best depth in $\{0.5,\ldots,64\}$ using its test labels under the same procedure.
Six prior post-processing methods use the same predictions and, except for the two threshold methods, the same not-background foreground.
We test field and boundary probability thresholds~\cite{waldner2020decode} and hierarchical merging by mean boundary probability along shared borders~\cite{arbelaez2011hierarchical,persello2019delineation}, along with stochastic watershed~\cite{angulo2007stochastic}, iterative marker depth~\cite{koyuncu2016iterative}, the oriented watershed with a hierarchy level of Zhu et al.~\cite{zhu2024gfafd}, and the Gaussian-mixture thresholds of Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025earlyseason}, fitted per country and followed by subtracting the thinned boundary mask.
For each, we search its parameter grid on PlanetScope B3 and report test results for the setting with the highest country-averaged score on the \emph{validation} split.
We choose $h$ and $\tau$ for BoundaryVote the same way, with the minimum-size step in place because its over-segmentation leaves slivers without it, and reuse every setting unchanged on Sentinel-2.

\paragraph{Metrics}
We pair predicted and reference polygons one at a time at intersection over union (IoU) 0.5, where IoU is their shared area divided by their combined area.
Recognition quality (RQ) measures field detection as the number of matched polygons divided by the average number of predicted and reference polygons.
Segmentation quality (SQ) measures shape accuracy as the mean IoU of matched polygons, and we compute PQ as their product~\cite{kirillov2019panoptic}.
We pool patches within each country, then give all ten countries equal weight in the macro average.
We also report PQ and RQ over the reference parcels under 0.5~ha, the small bin of the FTP evaluation code and the largest of its three bins.
The miss rate is the fraction of reference fields with no prediction covering half of their area, and the merge rate the fraction of predictions covering half of two or more reference fields.
All values are on a 0--100 scale.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:results}
BoundaryVote raises PQ on all four model and sensor pairs with the same minimum-size step as the FTP pipeline (Table~\ref{tab:main}).
Even selecting each country's best watershed depth on its test labels produces a smaller gain (Table~\ref{tab:compare}, $\Delta$Tune).
Resampling each country's test patches 1,000 times gives 95\% intervals for the gain whose lower bounds are at least \GainCILow{} points on every pair (supplementary material).
SQ, RQ, small-field PQ, the miss rate, and the merge rate all improve on every pair.
Relative to its starting point, PQ rises most for the smallest fields (Table~\ref{tab:main}), where smallholder mapping needs it~\cite{persello2023ai4smallfarms}.
On PlanetScope B3, PQ below 0.5~ha rises from \BaseSmall{} to \OursSmall{}, compared with \BaseLarge{} to \OursLarge{} above 2~ha, with the same ordering on all four pairs (supplementary material).
Cambodia has the smallest fields and gains most on average over the four pairs, while Portugal, with two test patches, has the only pair without a gain (Fig.~\ref{fig:percountry}).

\subsection{Comparison with Prior Post-Processing}
\label{sec:compare}
Only the oriented watershed of Zhu et al. also improves on the FTP pipeline (Table~\ref{tab:compare}), and like BoundaryVote only with the minimum-size step, since both over-segment the boundary probability and leave slivers until that step removes them (\OwtNoFilterPQ{} PQ without it).
The two share that over-segmentation, so the gap of \OwtGapPS{} points on PlanetScope and \OwtGapSS{} on Sentinel-2 isolates the decision rule: merging regions below one level of mean boundary strength against the vote along each line, which keeps more of the small fields (supplementary material).
Thresholding the two probability maps matches the FTP pipeline at negligible cost but leaves neighboring fields merged wherever a predicted boundary has a gap, and hierarchical merging scores borders by boundary probability as we do but against an absolute threshold rather than the field probability at the same pixel.
Selecting each country's best setting using its own test labels instead of the shared setting adds \OursTune{} points to BoundaryVote and at most \PriorTuneMax{} to any prior method.
BoundaryVote takes \OursSlowdown{} the FTP pipeline's time on dense patches, while stochastic watershed is \SwstSlowdown{} slower still because it repeats the watershed for each set of seeds.
Every method uses less than \PeakMB{}~MB of additional memory per patch on either sensor, so runtime determines the choice.

\subsection{Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}
Table~\ref{tab:ablation} separates the foreground, the watershed surface, and the vote, all with the minimum-size step.
Keeping boundary-class pixels without splitting merges neighboring fields and lowers PQ to \NbgNoneMinPQ{}, and the probability watershed with the vote gains little on the field-class foreground, because the boundary class already separates most fields and the small ones are gone.
On the not-background foreground, the vote applied to distance-map proposals at the FTP depth, our earlier form, reaches \DistancePQ{}.
Over-segmenting the boundary probability at the same seed depth without any vote gives \NoVotePQ{}, against \OursPlanetThree{} with the vote, and across the four model and sensor pairs the vote changes PQ by \VoteGainMin{} to \VoteGainMax{} points, so the gain does not come from the vote at a chosen depth.
Its value shows when every minimum seeds ($h=0$): PQ falls to \NoVoteZeroPQ{} without the vote and \OursZeroPQ{} with it, and the supplementary sweeps stay within half a point for $\tau$ from 0.1 to 0.5 and depths from 0.01 to 0.05.
Without the minimum-size step the over-segmentation is fatal, at \OursNoFilterPQ{} PQ, whereas the distance-map form loses \DistanceAreaGain{} points and the FTP pipeline \BaseAreaGain{}.
The released polygon extraction tool~\cite{kerner2024ftw} includes this threshold, although the published evaluation does not apply one.

\section{Conclusion}
BoundaryVote uses boundary-class pixels to recover discarded fields, a watershed of the boundary probability to propose splits, and a vote along each line to keep only the supported ones.
Together, those changes improve polygon accuracy over the FTP pipeline on two encoders and two sensors without per-region tuning, with the largest gain in the small fields needed for smallholder mapping.
The rule needs a predicted boundary class, so it does not apply to instance segmentation models that return only masks and scores.
